video.title: The Phone Habit That Was Ruining My Life

summary: Nick Huber and a guest (Corey) discuss breaking a phone addiction. Nick turned his phone off from 7pm to 7am, cut screen time to about 2.5 hours a day, batches texts and email into a 4:30-5pm calendar slot, and uses a notepad instead of his phone. The video contains no business idea; the takeaway is that managing attention and being hard to reach improves sleep, relationships and focus for a founder running several companies.

video.title: The BORING Way to Make $1M/Year Without a College Degree

summary: David Heacock interviews Jim Baloga, CEO and owner of three US proprietary schools (Porter and Chester Institute, YTI Career Institute, College of Court Reporting) that train skilled trades, healthcare and court reporting students. Baloga explains how he bought the court reporting school as a small platform to avoid a large US Department of Education letter of credit, then used it to acquire the larger schools he had run for about 20 years. He covers tuition, outcomes, regulatory barriers to entry, upfront cash collection, low acquisition multiples and a roll-up plan. The host's takeaway is that deep industry experience reveals opportunities, and that a trade skill is a low-risk base for entrepreneurship.

video.title: This guy beat the S&P500 for 11 years doing (almost) nothing

summary: A My First Million episode where the host recounts a retail investor (an exited founder) who made roughly 2.9 buy/sell decisions a year and claims ~21.8% annualised returns versus 13.5% for the S&P 500 over about 12 years. The hosts draw lessons on patience, circle of competence, pre-mortems (Jack Dorsey's '140 reasons Square will fail'), reversible vs irreversible decisions, and knowing 'what game you're playing'. The rest is anecdotes on Zuckerberg and Alexander Wang, Elon Musk's 'start building within 24 hours' story, motivation, and fear/panic management (the DARE method, rehearsal). There is no operating business idea; the value is in decision-making and mindset lessons.

speakers.name: Shaan Puri

tactics.name: Deep study of a few understandable companies, then wait for price
steps: Pick only a few companies you can understand.
Study them very deeply: read annual reports and keep detailed written notes over months.
Keep watching the company and wait until the price is cheap enough.
Buy on the day the opportunity appears; otherwise do nothing.

quote.text: I study a few things that I can understand. And I study them very deeply. I keep very detailed notes and then I just wait for an opportunity.
quote.speaker: Sam Parr

tactics.name: Pre-mortem before a big decision
steps: Before starting, write down every way it could fail (Dorsey wrote a list of 140 reasons Square would fail).
Use the list to design around those failure modes.
Judge decisions on the quality of the inputs or framework, not just the outcome (avoid 'resulting').

tactics.name: Sort decisions into reversible vs irreversible
steps: Classify each decision as reversible or not.
Do not agonise over reversible ones.
Spend thinking time only on the irreversible ones.

tactics.name: Rehearse the feared event in granular detail
steps: Recreate the real conditions in advance (same clothes, same meal, same environment), as George St-Pierre's coaches did.
Before a hard conversation such as a firing or negotiation, walk through the room and the motions beforehand.
Use exposure practice for phobias, such as short subway trips.

tactics.name: Define the game you are playing
steps: Ask yourself where you want to be in five years.
Name the game you are actually playing right now.
Let that game decide what you want and who you need to be, then ignore other games' metrics.

warnings.warning: Mistaking movement for progress: constant activity and agonising over small decisions can crowd out the few decisions that matter.

quote.text: we oftentimes mistake movement with progress.
quote.speaker: Sam Parr

warnings.warning: Don't judge decisions by outcomes alone (resulting); judge the input or framework.
Letting a failing business bleed into your daily life and routines (no trash can, air mattress) lowered productivity; fix routines first.
Beware the Dunning-Kruger overconfidence of early learners; the best admit how little they know.

lessons.lesson: Few, high-conviction decisions can beat constant activity; the reported investor averaged about 2.9 decisions a year and had three years with none.

quote.text: he only made 2.9 decisions a year.
quote.speaker: Sam Parr

lessons.lesson: Stay inside your circle of competence and be willing to say no to good opportunities you don't understand.
Write ideas down through pre-mortems and journals, and evaluate decisions on process rather than outcome.
Triage decisions by reversibility; don't agonise over reversible ones.
Investing rewards avoiding losses, while entrepreneurship rewards a few huge wins, so many mistakes are acceptable if the big bets pay off.
Strong leaders seek input widely from smart people, including less accomplished ones, and use the answers to gauge who gives high-signal advice.
Motion beats waiting for direction: start building quickly after a setback, since direction becomes clearer once you are in motion.

quote.text: It's about motion, not direction. And once you're in motion, it's a lot easier to figure out direction.
quote.speaker: Shaan Puri

lessons.lesson: When a business is struggling, stack small life wins (routine, exercise, tidy space) rather than waiting for outcomes to change.
Feared events are often worse in anticipation; rehearsal, acceptance and leaning into the feeling reduce fear.
Know the game you are playing; different games demand different traits and most people never define theirs.

evidence_quality.rationale: No business idea. The core investor claim (21.8% vs 13.5% annual return) is second-hand, anonymised, unverified and was recounted from a Claude analysis of his brokerage export. evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Includes a HubSpot-sponsored wealth guide plug; the hosts' own media business benefits from the content.

summary: UpFlip host visits Pat's King of Steaks in South Philadelphia, run by third-generation owner Frankie, who claims his family invented the Philly cheesesteak in 1930. The video covers the history, sourcing (imported frozen ribeye, Restaurant Depot, preservative-free), the kitchen workflow, a cook-off, and a candid Jan-Aug P&L showing roughly 18% net margin on about $3.9M revenue. Frankie advises that restaurant margins are thin and that the key to longevity is consistency of the original recipe, with add-ons and combos preferred over menu sprawl.

video.title: I built this app for my dad. Now it makes $18K/month

summary: Starter Story host Gus interviews Kurosh, a London-based product manager who built Boise (transcribed as 'Voice C'), a cross-platform dictation app using OpenAI's Whisper API, as a side project. It reportedly makes 16-20K USD per month including lifetime deals, with 11K MRR. He competes with well-funded tools like Whisper Flow by targeting seniors and people with disabilities, who see dictation as a painkiller rather than a vitamin. Growth comes mainly from SEO (about 200 blog posts, 30 landing pages, localisation), plus the Chrome Web Store, Reddit and a new YouTube series. Key takeaways: talk to users to discover your real customer, a crowded market can be won by serving a neglected niche, and take action in volume rather than strategising.

summary: Dark Horse Entrepreneur episode 565 argues that AI makes building apps fast but does not create demand, so aspiring micro-app founders should validate before building. It settles the 'validate vs copy an existing app' debate by saying existing apps prove a market but not that anyone will buy from you. It lays out a five-step test: micro-problem filter, proof checklist, switch conversation, smallest paid promise (pre-sale, do-it-by-hand, or specific waitlist), and a pre-set build/don't-build pass mark. The only worked example is a hypothetical $5/month game-day confirmation tool for youth cheer coaches.

warnings.warning: Do not ask 'would you use my app?'; people say yes because it costs them nothing.
Zero competitors and zero complaints usually means an empty road for a reason, not an open lane.
Set the pass mark before testing, or you will grade on a curve and move the goalposts.
Honour the refund if a pre-sale app does not ship; reputation cannot be rebuilt by AI.
Treat YouTubers' income claims as their story, not your forecast; avoid gaming votes or buying fake downloads.
Do not pitch in communities that ban promotion; ask questions instead.

lessons.lesson: Existing paying competitors are evidence of a market, but you still need a specific reason for someone to switch.
Prefer evidence that cost people something (money, time, effort) over compliments or opinions.
Pre-commit to a numeric pass/fail threshold and deadline before running a test.
Ask about past behaviour, not future intentions, to get truthful customer answers.
Shrink offers to one feature for one specific person; vague 'help small businesses' ideas are too big.
Use AI as a brainstorming and sparring partner, but it cannot replace real customers.

quote.text: AI drafts but a human decides and you're the human.

Use customers' unedited words from complaints and reviews to write sales copy.

summary: Starter Story interviews 19-year-old Vadim, a non-coder who 'vibe coded' Vugola, an AI video clipping/editing SaaS, in about four months and launched around March. video.title: I Let Strangers Pitch Me Their Business Live

summary: The Koerner Office hosts a live pitch event in Utah. Ten strangers get 2 minutes to pitch and 10 minutes of critique from Chris Koerner, Nick and Brandon. The pitches range from an operating VA-funded massage business doing about $68k/month and a $1.5M ARR home-service marketing agency to pre-revenue ideas such as a seed cup, an NFC keychain, a containment diaper, a choose-your-path kids' letter subscription, an AI relationship app and mail-in cast iron cleaning. The hosts invested in or offered to help several, and the audience voted Go Seeds first, Pick a Path Letters second and Utah Veterans Massage third. The main takeaways are that distribution (especially paid ads and short-form video) is the recurring bottleneck, and that investors want proof of a repeatable process before funding. All numbers are unverified pitch claims.

video.title: 6 BORING Things You Buy Once and Rent Out Every Weekend (Back in Your Driveway by Monday)

summary: A listicle-style video pitching six asset-rental side businesses that live in a driveway and run on a Friday handover and Monday return: bounce house, party tents/tables/chairs, tool kits, portable hot tub, utility trailer and camper. For each it gives rental rates, purchase costs, payback periods, who books, handover and reset routines, and a 'moat' (insurance, paperwork, deposits). It includes a failure story about skipping deposit and photos, a three-filter selection framework and a composite 'Harry' narrative. Figures are mostly generic, second-hand or illustrative, and the story is a narrated composite, so treat numbers as claims. Key takeaway: buy a cheap used asset, require insurance, deposit and photos, and stagger seasonal assets.

summary: David Heacock, founder of Filterbuy (US air filter manufacturer, claimed ~150,000 filters/day and ~$25M/month revenue), shares five stages of building a boring business: commit long enough to learn, fund the constraint, build systems that preserve judgment, don't diversify before the core is ready, and build resilience and legacy. He recounts leaving Goldman, buying a declining $300k/yr business with debt, taking $50k salary for 7.5 years, and losing millions in 2021 by launching a freight company and buying an HVAC business while the core was doubling. Key takeaway: do the work yourself first, turn judgment into systems, and put capital into the core constraint rather than diversifying early.

summary: Nick Huber (Sweaty Startup) answers two questions in a short excerpt: how to find and manage business partners, and whether to focus on one business or branch out. He says partners are hard to find and fail for moral reasons or because the value equation is off, and that splitting equity too many ways in small businesses leaves nobody making money. He notes that only 3 of his 11 companies matter financially (power law), four are unprofitable, and that 8 of 10 wealthy people he knows focused on one business. He pivoted out of a brutal student moving and storage business into self-storage. Key takeaway: focus on a good business, pick partners carefully, and stay open to better opportunities as momentum builds.

summary: Aaron Fuks of Hyros (Denver) explains how he built a B2B referral-pipeline business for home service trades (siding, painting, electrical, landscaping). He cold calls and mass-texts businesses in adjacent trades, gets a real bid or project first, then uses it as proof to sell partner introductions to a client. Pricing moved from $150 per appointment to $6,000 for 10 intros plus a $250-500/month nurturing fee, with claimed revenue around $27K last month. Key takeaway: bring value first (a real bid), sell relationships rather than leads, and run it on GoHighLevel with minimal cost.

ideas.name: Referral pipeline / partner-introduction service for home service trades
ideas.one_liner: Cold call and text adjacent-trade businesses to find live bids, then sell tradespeople bundles of vetted referral partner introductions plus ongoing relationship nurturing.
ideas.business_model: Per-appointment fee, then packaged intros (10 for $6,000) plus monthly nurturing/management subscription
ideas.customer: Home service business owners (siding, painting, electrical, landscaping, interior design, general contractors) wanting referral partners in adjacent trades
ideas.problem: Trades want steady high-value jobs from upstream partners (roofers, builders, designers) but lead marketplaces are shared and poor quality, and cold outreach is hard and time-consuming.
ideas.offer: Introductions to referral partners who have live bids, guarantee of two real bids in the first 20 appointments, replacement partners if no quote is delivered in time, plus CRM-based relationship nurturing and storm/blast text automations.

pricing.model: Package of intros plus monthly management fee (originally per appointment)
pricing.notes: Pricing 4x'd after pivot to packages with guarantees. Close is a menu: 20, 40 or 120 appointments. Commission of ~30% paid to the caller per appointment.

acquisition_channels.details: Early on: Google Maps lists, 20-40 dials a day with a GoHighLevel power dialer, 15 second ring time, no voicemails, custom dispositions; roughly 2 appointments per day. Also calls immediately when someone replies to a text.

acquisition_channels.details: Mass text a few hundred partner businesses (e.g. 200 custom builders and luxury remodelers) asking if they have projects needing a specialist bid; 2-5% reply with a project; then text prospective clients saying a bid is available (10-15% response) and call replies immediately. Texts drip out to keep call volume manageable.

quote.text: we pulled a huge list of all the roofers in our area and we sent a text to every single one of them
quote.speaker: Aaron Fuks

About 90% profit, one commission-only caller taking ~30% per appointment
Painting client got 4 bids worth $17K-$64K within 48 hours, paid for about 3 years of nurturing fees
Revenue about $27K last month, up from $14K in June

ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Immediate; began earning per appointment within the first month of calling

acquisition.how: Texting and CRM drips are automatable, but UK PECR bars unsolicited texts to sole traders and many trades are sole traders; the human phone call to qualify and close is central. Cold email to limited companies and call screening against TPS/CTPS are lawful alternatives.

onboarding.how: Client onboarding is a sales call plus PDF blueprint and GoHighLevel sub-account setup; agents could handle the setup but closing relies on a human.

delivery.how: Qualifying partners and verifying bids needs human phone conversations; nurturing sequences and referral tracking are automated.

video.title: The ChatGPT Scam That's Too Good to Be True: Don't Get Caught!

summary: A short promotional teaser warning that people searching how to make money with ChatGPT are being targeted by malware, fake apps and fake browser extensions that steal ChatGPT logins. The speaker cites over 101,000 infected devices and about 27,000 credential sets sold on the dark web in a month. Stolen chat histories can expose business ideas, financial numbers and client details. The key takeaway is to verify the legitimacy of any AI opportunity or app before using it, and the full episode (linked in the description) covers what to check in your own ChatGPT account.

video.title: How To Sell Anything To Anyone Online (I Spent $1M Learning This)

summary: Codie Sanchez explains her '6M' framework for selling anything online, drawn from the launch of her second book (Owner Beyond ... ) via a free virtual event with a $1M giveaway. The Ms are: magnet (reciprocity/exclusivity/self-referencing ads), message (customer is the hero, benefit before feature), micro-commitment (get a small first yes, then upsell), make the ask (clear, longer CTAs with six rules), money (margin and owning customer data), and map (90/60/30/10 launch content calendar). Key takeaway: lead with a valuable free give, sell the customer's ideal state, step up asks gradually, and protect margin and customer ownership. Mostly marketing/launch advice rather than a specific business idea, and the claims are self-reported and promotional.

video.title: Forget Snack Machines. This One Refills Itself

summary: Chris Koerner interviews CJ, a Fort Worth operator of four outdoor ice and water vending machines (Everest, Cooler Ice, Twice the Ice, and a large Ice House America-style unit) with no employees beyond one part-time maintenance tech. CJ explains how he got in via his pool-service business's ice spend, why buying distressed existing machines and locations beats building from scratch, how revenue-share vs flat-rent leases work, and the claimed ~90% gross margins. He also covers sale multiples of 2-3x annual profit, avoiding financing, and low-cost entry from $500-$1,000 for a used small machine. Key takeaway: location and buying out stressed single-machine owners are the main levers, but the business needs physical servicing.

video.title: Unfortunately, Sales Really Is This Simple (4 Steps)

summary: Codie Sanchez explains a four-part sales framework: fix mindset (don't sell from your own wallet, sell from confidence not need), fix the message (current state, future state, bridge, with the buyer stating the gap and numbers), fix the proof (named, faced, specific testimonials plus anti-sales), and fix the avatar (find people already in pain, sell oxygen not dessert). She promotes her Boardroom community, an upcoming book and a HubSpot growth kit. Key takeaway: ask questions so the buyer sells themselves, price against the cost of the problem, and target buyers already feeling the pain.

Only then present your product as the bridge, restating their numbers

steps: State openly who should not buy

Instead of discounting, show the ROI or offer a more expensive option

lessons.lesson: Price against the cost of the problem the customer has, not against your own sense of what is affordable.

quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

lessons.lesson: Prioritise problems that are urgent and painful (oxygen) because those buyers find budget.

Neediness and 'circling back' language leaks a weak mindset; lead the buyer with choices and value instead.

video.title: Make Money With This New AI Agent That Works 24/7

summary: Chris Koerner tries the agentic AI tool he calls 'Grok Bot' for the first time and uses it to build a 'Morning Lock' product: a Mac menu bar app plus Chrome extension that locks Gmail and the Mail app outside set hours (e.g. 5-10am), with an accountability password held by a spouse. He had Claude write the prompt, then Grok Bot built, tested and fixed the app via Replit, GitHub and Stripe in about 31 minutes of recording. He says he plans to sell it as a SaaS in a part two, but no sales or revenue are shown. The takeaway is that agentic AI can produce a working, personally useful software product from one detailed prompt; whether it sells is untested.

summary: UpFlip host Paul visits Emily and Jeff of Lancaster Cupcake in Pennsylvania, a 15-year-old business that grew from home baking after a Ponzi-scheme loss and a $1,400 start to roughly $3.5M revenue. The video covers production (a $20k depositor, a $60k walk-in oven, up to 6,000 cupcakes a day), cupcake trucks, three retail sites, a full P&L showing about 40% claimed margin, and the Profit First cash-flow method. Marketing relies mainly on a 50,000-person email list and a loyalty program. A flavour-creation challenge fails comically. Key takeaway: a physical, labour-heavy product business with strong repeat-customer email marketing and disciplined cost control.

video.title: I Found the Perfect First Business for Introverts

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Ryan Schuetter, a 24-26 year old introverted Cincinnati ex-hospital project manager ($52k/yr) who now earns roughly $10-15k/month as an AI implementation consultant and educator. He started by having ~100-150 free, non-salesy video calls with people in his personal network and business groups, converting about 12 into paying clients (~$25k lifetime from the first 12). His offers are private AI coaching ($5-10k/month), month-long cohort groups ($1,000 per seat), and one-off implementation builds ($1k-$20k), organised around his DASA framework (Diagnose, Articulate, Systemize, AI). Key takeaway: relationship-led, value-first outreach plus education and free content can win clients without sales experience, though the model is human-led and network-dependent.

video.title: I Tried to Make $10K in 10 Days With Costco Returns

summary: Chris Koerner flies in Shannon, an experienced liquidation reseller, to teach him to buy Costco customer-return pallets via the B-Stock auction platform and resell them on Facebook Marketplace. They bid on two lots (18 pallets of appliances at about $243/unit and a 12-unit patio/shed/gazebo lot at about $222/unit landed) and then test, photograph, list and sell the items. Chris aimed for $10K profit in 10 days but took 12.5 days; exact final totals are not stated in the transcript. Key lessons: buy at a very low per-unit cost, list the best items first for momentum, respond fast, and cut prices when listings get no hits. This is hands-on physical work, not hands-off.

acquisition.how: Listing creation can be AI-assisted (ChatGPT titles and copy), but Facebook Marketplace has no sanctioned API for posting, and photos and video must be taken physically.

onboarding.how: Messenger chats can use templates, but buyers ghost and haggle, and pickup times need human coordination.

delivery.how: Physical pallets must be received, unwrapped, tested, cleaned, photographed, stored and handed over or delivered by a person.

billing.how: Cash and Venmo at handover, taken in person.

support.how: Occasional post-sale problems handled by the owner personally as goodwill; low volume but needs a human.

uk_applicability.notes: UK has equivalents (B-Stock UK, Costco UK liquidation pallets, Facebook Marketplace, eBay, Gumtree), but the Costco returns lots on B-Stock are US-centred. UK Consumer Rights Act applies to sales of used goods by traders, and sellers who resell regularly are trading, so need HMRC registration; electrical goods need PAT or safety care. Garage space and UK-sized appliances differ from the US.

risks: Condition grade uncertainty: some items arrive broken, missing parts or damaged

video.title: You Don’t Need to Start a Business, Buy One of These 10 Instead

summary: Johnny Robinson (Johnny & Sergio, Home Service Academy) ranks 10 business types to buy from F to S tier using one test: would the business survive if the owner walked away tomorrow? Ecommerce/FBA, founder-brand businesses and first-timer franchises rank worst; laundromats mid; lawn care, fence/deck, pest control, waste routes and HVAC/plumbing rank higher; small ageing-owner cleaning companies rank S tier. The key takeaway is to buy sticky recurring customer lists from owners with no exit plan, using seller financing, then add systems. The video ends in a pitch for his Home Service Academy coaching, so the ranking is promotional.

video.title: He Turned a Side Hustle Into a $130K/MO Cleaning Business (Fully Remote)

summary: Johnny and Sergio (Home Service Academy) interview their student Paul, who runs a remote cleaning business in Los Angeles alongside his 9-to-5 engineering/sales job. Started March 2024, he claims about $130K/month revenue after roughly two years. He explains why he chose cleaning (remote, AI-proof, recurring), how he grew it (reliable crews, phone sales, reviews, SEO, paid lead channels, a salesperson), and what was hard (finding crews, emotional swings). Key takeaway: the business is a crew-management and sales-call operation, and crew quality and recurring conversion drive results. The hosts sell the coaching program, so the claims are promotional.

The fullest case is Brandon's teenage son, who bought 115 auction rugs for about $1,500 and sold about 80 for over $3,000 to fund a first car. The fence story is second-hand and the others are mostly observed or hypothetical. The takeaway is that low-tech, rent-or-resell businesses have cheap entry and fast payback, but almost all need physical work.

video.title: 5 Ways to Make Money From an AI the Government Fears

summary: Chris Koerner says Anthropic's Fable 5 model was shut off worldwide three days after launch, after a US Commerce Department export-control letter. He claims its main strength is long-running autonomous work. He pitches five businesses to prepare now using weaker models: legacy code migration, overnight bookkeeping cleanup, an AI-staffed productized design studio, hyper-personalised email, and self-running website portfolios. Each is said to mirror an existing human-run business. The ideas are speculative and unvalidated, and the Fable claims are unverified. The takeaway is to build the niche, offer and landing page now with current models and not depend on a single AI tool.

video.title: 9 BORING Products I’d Sell If I Needed Money

summary: Tim Richard, an e-commerce founder, lists nine 'boring' product niches that he says have high Google search volume, low keyword difficulty and few dedicated brands. They are stainless steel litter boxes, hojicha latte, satin sheets, rice water shampoo, key fob covers, beef protein powder, men's crossbody bags, non-tarnish jewelry and floor couches. His method is to use social media and Ahrefs keyword data to find rising search trends, then build a branded site around one specific term. The picks are his own opinion, with no tested sales data for any of them. The video also promotes his paid 'idea book' database.

lessons.lesson: Search volume combined with low keyword difficulty and few dedicated brands is a cheap way to screen product niches before investing.
When Amazon or generic retailers rank first, Google lacks a dedicated brand for the term, which signals an opening for a focused site.
Where no advertisers bid, paid ads can bridge the gap while organic ranking builds.
Consumable products suit subscriptions, giving recurring revenue.
A single hero product aimed at an unmet search need (the Nugget Couch approach) beats a broad catalogue.
Keyword demand shows interest, not purchase intent or margin; it must still be validated with real sales tests, and search data is region-specific.
Higher-margin categories like jewelry give more room for ad spend.

evidence_quality.rationale: Listicle of the host's own opinions based on keyword tool data. No first-hand results for any listed product, and the revenue claims are generic and unverified. The search data is useful but probably US-based.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Host sells an 'idea book' database of 450+ opportunities and promotes it twice in the video.

video.title: He Made $60K His First Month With This Boring Business

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Mike from Iowa City, a tile installer who launched a garage-floor concrete coatings business (flake floors using polyurea base and polyaspartic top coat) around February-March 2026 with his brother and two experienced partners. He claims $60K revenue in April and $69K in May with over 50% profit, driven almost entirely by Meta ads, instant phone follow-up, upfront $8/sq ft pricing and a 10% deposit. Key takeaways: blue-collar service bars are low (answer the phone, show up, be transparent on price), AI (Claude) writes all ad copy and advises on ad budgets, and startup cost can be roughly $15-25K or under $1K by renting a grinder.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office

speakers.name: Mike
speakers.description: Tile contractor from Iowa City who runs Old Cap Coatings (concrete coatings) with partners; one of four partners

ideas.name: Garage floor flake coatings (Old Cap Coatings)
ideas.one_liner: Grind, coat and flake residential garage floors with polyurea base and polyaspartic top coat at $8/sq ft, one-day jobs, sold via Meta lead ads.
ideas.business_model: Per-job price per square foot with 10% non-refundable deposit; balance paid after the job.
ideas.customer: Mostly homeowners aged 50+, typically male, with 2-4 car garages; also some interior, patio, pool deck and commercial (a church, a warehouse).
ideas.problem: Bare or pitted concrete garage floors look bad and stain; owners want a decorative, easy-clean, durable finish.
ideas.offer: Decorative flake garage floor (grind, polyurea base coat, broadcast flake, polyaspartic top coat) installed in one day by a two-person crew, with optional move-your-stuff add-on.

pricing.model: Flat $8 per sq ft for everything, published in ads; add-ons for steps and stem walls

price_points.label: Optional extra to have contents moved

pricing.notes: Premium vs competitors; one competitor about 50% cheaper. Little discounting; 10% off offered for winter interior bookings. Credit card accepted, no financing.

acquisition_channels.details: Meta (mostly Facebook, targeted 55+ males) lead-form ads showing grinding and flake-throwing video (~23 seconds); 80-90%+ of leads. Best ad hook is brother asking 'how much does it cost?' with price stated. Added one qualifying question (interior/garage/exterior/other). Spend about $200/day, doubled to $400/day for second crew; 50-mile radius.

quote.text: it's all basically all meta ads. Yeah. We get some Google traffic. We have a referral program, but it's mostly meta.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Google Local Services Ads used alongside; modest traffic. Not on Thumbtack or Angi.
First three jobs came from friends/church at early-bird discount; $200 referral program produced a ~$30K warehouse job; happy customers recommend contractors.

quote.text: That $200 referral turned into like a $30,000 job cuz we got his mom to do it.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Ask for reviews so the Google Business Profile ranks naturally.

ideas.delivery: Two-person crew (lead at about $35/hr, helper about $25/hr, W2, paid 40 hours/week) grinds floor with a propane 20-inch grinder and vacuum, rolls polyurea base, broadcasts flake, scrapes, applies polyaspartic top coat in a ~10-hour day. Mike does about 1-2 hours/day oversight; brother Luke does phone sales and in-person quotes; two partners are the field experts. Second crew and Des Moines expansion planned.
unit_economics_claims: Materials about $2.06/sq ft (stated as $1.56 base/flake/top plus ~$0.50 misc); overhead about $1/sq ft; labour about $0.80/sq ft; total about $3.90/sq ft versus $8 price
April revenue $60K, May about $69K, profit over 50%
Cost per lead $30 (best ad) to $100; about 20% close rate
One job can yield $3-4K profit in a day
Targeting $1M revenue in first year
ideas.startup_cost: About $22-25K as done (including $10K used U-Haul box truck, ~$1K logo, grinder, vacuum); can trim to $15-20K with electric grinder; under $1,000 theoretically by renting a grinder (~$300/day, ~$1K/week) and doing one job.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: First test job in February 2026 (own garage), three paid early-bird jobs within weeks; paid advertising began March; fully booked from April.

acquisition.how: Meta ad creative copy and budget tuning are done with Claude and can be agent-managed, though video content of real jobs and a human calling leads at once are needed.

onboarding.how: Instant phone call to lead, in-person measuring/quoting and deposit; mostly human salesperson.

delivery.how: Physical grinding, coating and flaking by a two-person crew.

billing.how: 10% deposit then payment on completion via card/Venmo/cheque; invoicing and payment links are easily automated.

support.how: Warranty failures and redo jobs require crews on site; customer questions handled by phone.

uk_applicability.notes: Resin flooring exists in the UK but garages are smaller and less common as a status upgrade, so ticket sizes and demand will be lower, and prices would be in GBP per m2. UK weather and damp slabs matter. No contractor licence needed in general, but insurance applies. Meta lead ads and Google LSA-style channels work; GDPR/PECR needs care for calling leads who opted in (acceptable with consent).

risks: Failed floor from wrong product required a full regrind and redo
Physical, weather and humidity dependent; scheduling slips
Low barriers may attract competition drawn by visual ads
Quality and prep variability per garage; reliable crew hiring
Claims are very recent (2-3 months of data)

video.title: The Simplest AI Side Hustle for Beginners

summary: Chris Koerner shows a beginner AI side hustle for garage door repair owners: build an instant quote generator and a job profit tracker with Lovable (no code), plus an after-hours AI voice answering agent in GoHighLevel. He scrapes about 513 Google Maps listings with Outscraper for $111, filters to mobile numbers, cold-texts 50 owners via Straight Text, and gets roughly 40-50% replies and one 'yes' within an hour. He pitches $50 per closed lead with no upfront cost and extrapolates to $100k/month, which is hypothetical. Key takeaway: lead with a low-risk offer, validate with real outreach before building, and use no-code/AI tools to ship fast. Lovable is a channel sponsor and the cold SMS method is illegal in the UK for sole traders.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; demonstrates the build and outreach live.

ideas.name: AI after-hours voice answering agent for garage door repair companies
ideas.one_liner: Set up a GoHighLevel AI voice agent that answers missed after-hours calls for garage door repairers, captures name and address, and charges per closed lead or a monthly fee.
ideas.business_model: Per-lead fee (pitched $50 per closed lead) with possible later monthly retainer; Chris also mentions $20-$200 per lead or hundreds per month.
ideas.customer: Owners of small garage door repair businesses (Dallas-Fort Worth in the demo) who miss after-hours calls.
ideas.problem: Owners are on job sites or off duty with phones on silent, so after-hours leads go to voicemail and are lost to competitors; 78% of customers hire the first company to quote.
ideas.offer: A 24/7 AI voice agent that answers calls, collects name and address, emails a call summary and transcript, and can forward urgent callers to the owner. Free setup, no contract, pay only when a lead closes.

pricing.model: Pay per closed lead (test offer), possibly monthly retainer later
pricing.notes: Chris says he may add contracts, upfront money or a retainer later; the first offer is deliberately low-risk.

acquisition_channels.details: Scraped Google Maps with Outscraper, kept mobile numbers only, and bulk-texted 50 owners from Straight Text with a short message ('Hey, I'm here in Dallas. Do you still fix garage doors? I found you on Google Maps'), then sent the pitch to those who replied.

quote.text: Do you answer your phone after hours? The reason I ask is because I created an AI voice agent that will
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Google Maps listings used as the lead source, not as an inbound channel.

ideas.delivery: Agent built in GoHighLevel's Voice AI with a custom prompt/knowledge base generated by ChatGPT. Each client gets a dedicated or ported phone number, a workflow forwards urgent callers to the owner (with secondary and tertiary fallbacks), and emails with transcripts go to agency and owner.
unit_economics_claims: Setup took a couple of minutes; GoHighLevel AI employee has a 30-day free trial
Total validation spend under $100 (scrape plus texting software)
Extrapolation: 200 customers x $500/month = $100k/month (hypothetical)
ideas.startup_cost: Under $100 to validate (scrape cost $111 in the demo, GoHighLevel 30-day free trial for the AI employee)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: not stated; first 'yes' reply came in under an hour but no money was collected

acquisition.how: Lead scraping and list cleaning can be scripted, but the demonstrated channel is unsolicited SMS, which is unlawful in the UK for sole traders and individuals under PECR. A legal UK version would use cold email to limited companies or inbound ads/SEO, and replies would still need a human or agent to handle.

onboarding.how: Agent creation, number provisioning and prompt generation are largely templated; a human checks the knowledge base and ports numbers.

delivery.how: Once configured, the voice agent answers calls, logs transcripts and forwards urgent calls with no human involvement; occasional prompt tuning is needed.

billing.how: Per-closed-lead billing needs the owner to report which leads closed, which is hard to automate; a flat monthly fee via Stripe would be near-unattended.

support.how: Owners will need help with call handling and disputes over lead attribution; AI can handle first-line questions.

uk_applicability.notes: Voice agents work in the UK, but the cold SMS method breaches PECR for sole traders; UK suppliers would use limited-company cold email or TPS-screened calls. Call-recording and AI disclosure rules (UK GDPR) apply. Market is smaller and Google Maps categories differ.

video.title: The Best Side Hustle for Beginners (Any Age)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews two college-age resellers, Lucas and John, from rural North Carolina/Virginia, who started on eBay selling childhood Legos and thrift-store finds, then moved into bulk consumer electronics. They describe buying 500-unit lots from a European supplier, a bad batch that lost about $4-5k, and diversifying into US suppliers via about 1,000 cold calls and 12,000 emails. They claim six figures of revenue last year and say anyone can make $1,000-5,000 a month with 2-5 hours a week. Key takeaway: reselling starts with low risk (sell your own stuff, thrift, Facebook Marketplace to eBay), but sourcing is the bottleneck and supplier concentration is dangerous.

video.title: The Beginner-Friendly Claude AI Side Hustle Nobody Talks About

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Ryan Dozer, a solo AI marketer who runs a six-figure SEO/content agency. Dozer explains Claude skills (markdown SOPs for AI agents) and how he packaged about 20-25 of his own into a $99 'Claude Code skill stack' sold from his own site via Stripe, claiming over $3,000 in 30-45 days. He demonstrates an SEO blog-post-writer skill that turns YouTube videos into ranking articles, a LinkedIn scraper skill using Apify, and a vibe-coded marketing OS. Key takeaway: turn the workflows and expertise you already use daily into skills and sell them as digital products, but the numbers are self-reported and the sales path leans on his existing audience.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jay Meldrum, who left corporate professional services to open Swing Cave Golf, a single-bay members-only golf simulator in a Texas strip mall (Allen area). Six months in he has about 28 members on three tiers (USD 175/275/325 per month), roughly USD 7,000 monthly revenue, break-even at about 15 members after three months, and claimed 50-55% net margins. The business is run with 24/7 app-based door access, scheduling software and cameras, with about an hour a week of owner time. Upfront cost is about USD 100K, and he plans a second location and eventual scaling. Takeaway: a low-opex, membership-based, physical-space business can be near-passive once built, but it needs significant capital and a physical site.

summary: Chris Koerner explains how to start and run a farmer's market (using his wife's kids' market at a shopping centre as the example), then interviews Mike McCoy of Prep Pizza, who sold DIY pizza dough kits at farmer's markets (about $60k in a first summer, part time) before scaling online via Facebook ads to claimed $3-4M of sales. The video also covers other farmer's market products (baked goods, pickles, fresh pasta) and tips such as sampling, choosing in-city markets, and filming content. Key takeaway: farmer's markets are a cheap, fast way to validate a physical food product, and a market organiser can piggyback on a venue that wants footfall.

video.title: He Can't Code but His AI Agents Make Him $5K/Month

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Vadim, an 18-year-old non-coder who vibe-coded Vugola, an all-in-one clipping, scheduling and captioning SaaS, using Claude Code, Supabase, Vercel and GitHub. He claims $5K revenue in 30 days at ~80% margin, with 267 paying users on $9/$39/$99 plans, acquired mainly via Twitter after Reddit/X outreach by an OpenClaw agent. He also describes running a small team of Hermes agents (CEO, marketing, growth, coding, support) and shares prompting tips, PostHog analytics, Paperclip, and mind-mapping for niche research. Key takeaway: a solo founder can build and run a niche SaaS with AI agents cheaply, but the numbers are self-reported and the product is still in beta.

video.title: This AI Finds Cheap Products You Can Sell for 5x More

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates going from a physical product idea to a sourced product in one sitting, using the AI sourcing agent Accio (transcribed 'Axio'). He validates demand for a discreet 'porch pirate' parcel box via Google Trends, searches Accio in natural language, generates a tech pack, and compares supplier prices to Amazon listings. He claims a $27 sourced box sells for $143 on Amazon, about 75-80% gross margin and 20-30% net after shipping and fees. The video is sponsored by Accio, so the takeaway is that sourcing and validation tools make starting a physical product business faster, but the numbers are an unverified back-of-envelope demo.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews David (Fort Wayne, Indiana), a 'multipreneur' running several small rental businesses. He details a tote (moving box) rental business sold via a realtor gifting subscription, a travel-trailer (RV) rental business that made about $7,000 net in its first season, and a side-hustle recording/video studio. The takeaway is that small rental businesses need little capital, reuse the same asset repeatedly, and can be validated by asking existing operators and using marketplaces as lead-gen before moving customers to your own site.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Sariah (27, Utah), who started Memory Magnets Co with under $1,000 in 2024 after her husband's low pay and second job left the family broke. She sells custom photo magnets online, at markets and as an on-the-spot wedding/event service, and sells magnet-making machine kits plus refill supplies and courses. She claims $1.63M online revenue in her first full year (about $600K profit), a $233K best month and a $100.5K first six-figure month after six months. Key takeaway: a simple, high-margin physical product plus a service at price-insensitive events (weddings), marketed through short-form video, grew fast, and teaching others to copy the model became a second revenue line.

video.title: How to Get Your First Service Clients Paying Tens of Thousands

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jamison, a former private-equity professional who launched West Coast Decks in Southern California with no trade experience. He closed $60,000 of jobs in month one using paid lead services, and says he reached just under $1M in year one and now does $4-8M a year. The video is a tactical playbook for launching a high-ticket home service business: pick a low-decision-count, high-order-value niche, invest in branding early, respond to leads in seconds, hire a well-paid VA, cultivate referrals from adjacent trades via social media, and bid at 50% gross margin (2x COGS).

Posts daily on Instagram and Facebook plus an email newsletter; consistent branding and profiles on Google, Yelp, Houzz, BBB and Chamber of Commerce.

Instagram-driven referrals from other trades (mostly landscapers, roofers) said to produce about $400k in year one and $600k in year two; also meets lumber yards and supplier sales reps in person who send leads.
No ads for the first 3 years; PPC, Google LSA and Meta ads are a 2026 initiative.

ideas.delivery: Installed physically by crews; California in-house versus subcontractors is tricky, he says either works if managed well. Installs about half a million sq ft of decking per year.

video.title: How To Get Paid $2,500 + Monthly Checks for "Drag & Drop" AI Employees

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Danny, a member of his TK Owners community, who builds AI voice agents (on Go High Level) for local businesses such as barbers. He built a free missed-call voice agent and website for his own barber, which produced a referral chain and several inbound calls from barbers. Danny plans to charge $2,500-$5,000 upfront plus $200-$500 per month. His sales method is to build a Replit website mockup or a live voice agent demo before the first meeting, then reconnect a week or two later to close. The takeaway is to start with a free, high-quality build for someone in your circle and use the result as a showcase and referral source.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; runs TK Owners and Playmakers communities and promotes Go High Level via an affiliate link

speakers.name: Danny
speakers.description: Agency founder building voice agents and websites for local businesses; started about 11 years ago optimising Yelp profiles; has e-commerce and M&A background

ideas.name: AI voice agent (missed-call answering) for barbers and appointment-based local businesses
ideas.one_liner: Replace a busy barber's voicemail with a Go High Level voice agent that answers questions and texts a booking link, sold with a website and KPI dashboard.
ideas.business_model: Upfront setup fee plus monthly maintenance retainer
ideas.customer: Busy solo barbers and other appointment-based local businesses (salons, nails, massage), often in salon suites; also home inspection, remodeling and other local firms
ideas.problem: Barbers cutting hair cannot answer calls and miss new-customer bookings; voicemail loses leads
ideas.offer: A voice agent trained on the business's website or Google Business Profile that picks up when the owner does not answer, answers FAQs and opening hours, and texts the booking link. Bundled with a new website, KPI dashboard, SMS marketing, newsletters and reactivation tools.

pricing.model: Upfront setup fee plus monthly fee, customised per client

price_points.label: range of willingness to pay from other prospects

pricing.notes: Danny says the range depends on the client's understanding of the value and their stage; he avoids charging startups with no money. His first barber got it free in exchange for being a test case and referral source.

acquisition_channels.details: Free build for his own barber produced a referral from a medical-practice client in the same salon suite building, plus four or five calls in a week from barbers introduced by that one free customer. No ad or sponsorship spend.

quote.text: I haven't spent anything on ads. I haven't spent anything on on sponsorships or anything like that.
quote.speaker: Danny

acquisition_channels.details: Walk into barber shops, ask if they have heard of voice agents, and demo live by calling the number while they cut hair. Chris suggests changing the business name in the agent on your phone to the prospect's name and calling them. Also demoed to neighbouring salon staff in the shared building.
Danny found his tools and training through Koerner's TK Owners community. Sphere of influence (own barber, oil-change person, family) is the starting point.
Pre-built Replit website mockup made before the first meeting, after researching the prospect's current site with ChatGPT; reconnect in a week or two to close.

ideas.delivery: Danny does sales and vision; a coding-capable business partner handles integrations and fixes. The voice agent is set up in Go High Level by linking the website or Google Business Profile, connected to the client's work number so it answers when the owner does not pick up (rings first, then the agent). Replit builds the website and KPI dashboard. Danny says setup takes just a few clicks.
unit_economics_claims: $2,500 to $5,000 upfront plus $200 to $500 per month
Goal of 20 clients as passive income
First barber would pay about $2,500 upfront and $200 a month
125 missed calls handled on the test account since the number was created
ideas.startup_cost: Low; the first build was done for free on a Go High Level account supplied by Koerner. Ongoing Go High Level cost not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: not stated; first customer was free, paid pricing is still being set

acquisition.how: The main acquisition is in-person demos at shops and referrals. Inbound content or ads could be automated, but cold DMs to sole traders would breach PECR, so little of the described method is automatable.

onboarding.how: Agent can be trained from a website or Google profile with a few clicks; an agent could gather business info, but number porting and call-forwarding setup need some human checks.

delivery.how: Once configured the voice agent handles calls and texts links unattended; builds of sites and dashboards are agent-assisted but need occasional human fixes.

billing.how: Go High Level supports subscriptions and invoicing; the setup invoice is simple.

support.how: Agent transcripts allow monitoring; clients still need occasional script or knowledge updates and human handling of complaints.

uk_applicability.notes: The model works in the UK, since barbers, salons and UK telephony numbers can be linked to Go High Level. Changes needed: UK call recording/AI disclosure and GDPR consent for transcripts, UK number forwarding, GBP pricing, and the agent should disclose that it is an AI to be safe. Cold outreach to sole traders is restricted by PECR, so in-person selling or inbound is safer.

risks: Windows of opportunity close as competition and easier tools arrive
Low ticket size per barber limits revenue per client
Agent in the demo posed as a human; it may need to disclose it is AI
Reliance on Go High Level pricing and reseller terms
Medical or higher-stakes practices need human handoff
Replit builds can stall and need a coder to finish

summary: Chris Koerner shares a mindset framework (GRIT) drawn from 17 years and 80+ businesses, describing the downsides of entrepreneurship: Grind, Risk, Isolation, Turbulence. He pairs each with an antidote: Gratitude, Reminders, Interaction, Traction. The video contains no detailed business model; the only business idea is a brief mention of local newsletters, which coincides with a Beehiiv sponsor read. Key takeaway: entrepreneurship is emotionally volatile, so spread risk, stay connected, and notice small wins.

video.title: Forget Dropshipping. Be The Middleman For $800+/Job (Drop-Servicing)

summary: Chris Koerner tours a concrete-leveling (polyurethane foam lifting) operation in Houston with Jeff, a W-2 employee and father who started 90 days earlier and subcontracts all the physical work. Jeff claims almost $20k revenue, 30-40% gross margins and a $2,500 average job. He gets leads via Facebook ads, Nextdoor, Google, referrals, a Replit-built site with chatbots and HighLevel texting, and quotes jobs remotely from photos. Koerner shows the maths that about 36 leads a month and about 5 quoting hours a week could yield $10k/month profit. Key takeaway: a drop-servicing model, where you sell, quote and coordinate while insured subcontractors do the work, can run part-time, though the claims are early-stage and self-reported.

They discuss how vibe coding in AI Studio makes it nearly free to build and ship many small AI apps, and they live-build two apps: a video analysis engine and a voice AI lead-gen agent. video.title: The Most Copy-Pastable Online Business (Thanks to AI)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews a Dubai-based builder (name not stated in the transcript) who uses AI coding tools (Cursor, Claude Code) to build programmatic-SEO directory sites. His recipe site Guilty Chef ranks for restaurant-inspired recipes and reportedly gets about 11,000 organic visits a month and about $700-800 a month. His Best Dubai directory ranks near Tripadvisor for restaurant review searches. He demos a scaffold from his own product, 5 Day Sprint, building a protein snacks directory page live, and shows how to duplicate a project to launch more niche sites. The key takeaway is that AI makes niche directory sites cheap to build and clone, but SEO needs patience and the revenue shown is small.

video.title: You Can Start This $1M/Yr Business With No Tools and No Crew

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Rex Lindsay, owner of Cozy Pros, a Phoenix home-performance business selling attic insulation removal/re-insulation, Aeroseal duct sealing, duct cleaning and air scrubbers, mostly via Facebook ads offering a free attic inspection. Rex says he moved from ~100 in-house employees to subcontracting nearly all installation work, with a project manager on site, citing lower insurance, equipment and quality-risk burden. He gives average ticket (~$10k), margin structure (~52% gross, 15-20% net target), lead cost (~$75) and ad return claims. Key takeaway: learn lead generation and sales, subcontract the labor, and use cheap front-end offers (duct cleaning, free inspection) to upsell large tickets.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews 23-year-old Kyler, who rents used washers and dryers to renters via Facebook Marketplace in Utah, claiming about $10K/month with 120+ sets, no employees and 5-10 hours a week. His 'Post, Rent, Buy' process validates demand with a listing before buying any machines. Used Whirlpool direct-drive sets are sourced free or cheap, and he also covers appliance delivery for used-appliance shops as a side income. The video ends with a plug for Kyler's paid school community and Chris's TK Owners community.

summary: Chris Koerner live-validates a business in about 56 minutes: an AI after-hours voice answering service for home service businesses, starting with garage door repair companies in Dallas-Fort Worth. He scrapes Google Maps leads with Outscraper, cleans them in Google Sheets, keeps mobile numbers, bulk-texts 50 owners via Straight Text, then pitches a pay-per-closed-lead offer. He builds a demo voice agent in GoHighLevel in minutes. He gets about a 40-50% response rate and one 'yes' (interested), then extrapolates to a hypothetical $1.2M/yr. Key takeaway: validate demand with outreach before building anything, though the one yes is not a closed sale and the texting method is problematic in the UK.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office, running the experiment solo on camera in Dallas-Fort Worth.

ideas.name: AI after-hours voice answering for garage door repair companies
ideas.one_liner: Sell an AI voice agent that answers missed after-hours calls for local garage door repair businesses, charging per closed lead or a monthly retainer.
ideas.business_model: Per closed lead (test offer $50) or flat monthly retainer; possible per-lead $20-$200 or hundreds per month.
ideas.customer: Owners of small local garage door repair companies (high-ticket home service, not private-equity-consolidated) in DFW, extendable across the US.
ideas.problem: Owners do not answer the phone after hours and lose jobs worth hundreds to thousands of dollars; competitors send callers to voicemail.
ideas.offer: A 24/7 AI voice agent that answers, captures name and address, emails a call summary and transcript, and can forward urgent calls to the owner. Free setup, no contract, no upfront money, pay $50 only when a lead closes.

pricing.model: Pay-per-closed-lead in the test pitch; alternatives of per-lead fee ($20-$200) or monthly retainer, with possible contracts and upfront fees later.
pricing.notes: Price deliberately kept risk-free so price does not decide whether the test fails; to be raised later.

acquisition_channels.details: Scraped Google Maps numbers, kept mobile only, texted 50 owners via Straight Text with a short under-160-character message ('Hey, I'm here in Dallas. Do you still fix garage doors? I found you on Google Maps'), with a city name as a variable, then sent the pitch only to those who replied.

quote.text: I'm just trying to validate that they own the business that I think they own first. We'll get to the sales pitch later.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition.how: Lead scraping and list cleaning are automatable, but bulk unsolicited SMS to owners (many sole traders) is not lawful in the UK without consent. UK would need cold email to limited companies, TPS-screened calls, or inbound/SEO, and replies need human or agent handling.

summary: Chris Koerner demos OpenAI's new ChatGPT Agent mode, running six agents at once on business tasks: finding Nashville plumbers with websites, hyper-personalised cold emails to Austin dentists, competitor research for his Texas Snacks store, Google Trends ranking of business ideas, a calendar meeting-briefing task, and Amazon-review research that became a pitch deck. He pitches selling websites or SEO to businesses that already have websites, and selling AI-driven research to clients. He rates each task out of 10 and notes friction: logins, glitches when he navigated away from the tab, and slow runs. Takeaway: agents save hours of research and drafting, but need specific prompts, reference data and some supervision.

summary: Chris Koerner presents five low-capital businesses that sit around the hot tub industry rather than in hot tub manufacturing: hot tub inspection, custom spa covers, hot tub moving, hot tub rentals, and Airbnb hot tub cleaning/maintenance. Each is backed by case studies (mostly second-hand, found online or on Reddit) with revenue and pricing claims. He gives a validation playbook built on local Facebook groups, a Google Business Profile, a one-page website and cheap start-up. He closes by arguing that 'sweaty', non-AI businesses will gain demand as more people chase AI.

summary: A mindset-focused conversation between Chris Koerner and Shannon Gene (a reseller and content creator, speaking from Northern California) about the foundations of entrepreneurship: falling in love with problem solving, embracing fear and change, having 'delusions of grandeur' backed by action, and building a bias for action driven by curiosity and quick dopamine rewards. Koerner describes validating a private pickleball club in his metal shop with a $1.78-per-lead Facebook ad test, and Shannon Gene covers manual-before-automation lessons from Poshmark, Amazon self-publishing and obscure-parts reselling. The key takeaway is to start small, do things manually first, validate demand cheaply with math and act quickly. Few numbers are given and most are anecdotal.

video.title: If People Pay for This, Your Idea Will Work Too

summary: Chris Koerner and a co-host brainstorm business ideas built around the theme that people will pay for almost anything, and that ego stops people from doing weird, attention-getting things. Ideas include novelty competition events (horse haircut show, Excel esports, vibe-coding competitions, survival challenges), a plaque-selling service triggered by magazine features, a YouTube-to-print-magazine service, and quirky marketing stunts such as a realtor 'ghost free guarantee'. Evidence is mostly brainstorming and second-hand anecdotes, with few verified numbers. Key takeaway: memorable, talk-worthy content or events can create demand and customers in otherwise boring niches.

video.title: Fastest Way to Copy Winning Digital Products (Picsart)

summary: Chris Koerner shows how to find and copy winning digital products on Etsy. The old-school method sorts printables by top reviews and looks for sellers with many reviews but few products, cross-checked on Google Trends. The faster hack changes 'star' to 'best' in the Etsy filter URL to reveal hidden best-sellers. He then uses Picsart's AI enhance and image generation to create similar designs, tests them on Facebook Marketplace or $20 Facebook ads, and moves winners to Etsy. The key takeaway is to copy what already works and change nothing at first.

ideas.business_model: One-off digital product sales (instant download printables) on Etsy, net of Etsy fees
ideas.customer: Etsy shoppers buying printables: wall art, junk journals, baby shower games, coloring pages, stickers, homework pages

ideas.offer: Printable designs closely modelled on proven best-sellers, with AI-generated variations (e.g. seasonal wall art such as an Easter bunny)

pricing.model: Per-download price set near the proven best-seller; not specified
pricing.notes: No specific price given; the baby shower game price is only a guessing game in the video

acquisition_channels.details: List on Etsy and use Etsy's own search; use Etsy Ads on printables since the only cost is time/ad spend against a near-zero marginal product cost; optionally buy an established Etsy account whose feedback the algorithm already favours.

ideas.delivery: Digital instant download. Designs are created in Picsart using AI enhance and AI image generation, using a best-seller screenshot as the style reference, then listed with multiple mock-up pictures. Delivery to the buyer is automatic via Etsy.

Etsy Ads cost to acquire a customer is bounded by product price less Etsy fees

acquisition.how: Etsy search, Etsy Ads and Facebook ads are inbound and software-run, so agents can do most of it. Research scraping can be done by agents (Manus/Operator), but the Etsy URL hack may be fragile and Etsy's terms may restrict scraping.

onboarding.how: Buyers purchase and download instantly with no onboarding.

delivery.how: AI generates designs and listing images, and Etsy delivers the files. A human or vision-checked review is needed for quality, text errors and copyright similarity.

support.how: Low volume of buyer messages and refund questions; an agent can handle most with occasional human approval.

uk_applicability.notes: Etsy operates in the UK and sellers can list digital goods. UK VAT on digital sales needs handling (Etsy collects VAT in many cases), and HMRC trading income must be declared. Seasonal holidays differ (e.g. Easter works, Thanksgiving does not).

Review counts are a proxy for sales, not a guarantee

summary: Chris Koerner and Sam Thompson brainstorm business ideas enabled by ChatGPT's new image generation. They argue standalone novelty products (custom coloring books, print-on-demand art) are real but short-lived, and that the bigger opportunity is selling AI-generated personalised before/after mockups to home-service businesses (landscaping, painting, tree trimming, pool, remodel) for direct-mail and sales use. The pitch is a ~$500/month mockup tool or service sold to local contractors, found via Valpak mailers, plus tracked-number revenue-share deals. Key takeaway: the best marketer and channel wins, and the B2B application is less obvious than consumer novelty products. All numbers are speculative and untested.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Max Brodeur, co-founder of Y Combinator-backed Gumloop, a drag-and-drop AI workflow automation platform described as an AI-first Zapier. Max demos internal workflows (lead enrichment on signup, support-chat digest, pre-meeting research, SEO keyword filtering, YouTube-to-blog, Meta ads competitor analysis). Chris pitches businesses built on top: Gumloop expert/freelance builder, Facebook ads reverse-engineering as a service, programmatic SEO as a service, white-labelled flows. The key takeaway is that niche workflow knowledge encoded into AI workflows can be sold as a service, but the video is partly promotional (affiliate link) and numbers are sparse.

video.title: How This "NICHE DIRECTORY" Website Makes $10M/Year!

summary: Niche Pursuits host Spencer Haws reviews five niche directory websites: HappyCow (vegan restaurants, estimated $10M/yr by Growjo), SoakOregon (Oregon hot springs, ~30k visits/month), Sober Nation (rehab directory, ~$250k/yr across a small network, plus an SEO agency for rehab directories), Care.com (acquired for $500M) and MCP.so (MCP server directory, 3 months old, ~52k visits/month). Revenue figures are mostly estimates from Growjo, SimilarWeb traffic and an ad RPM calculator rather than verified numbers. The key takeaway is that niche directories monetise via display ads and sponsored placements, and that a directory can lead into an adjacent service business. A Hostinger sponsor segment is included.

video.title: The 4 Best Rural Side Hustles for 2026

summary: Chris Koerner throws a dart at a map of Texas, lands near Flatonia/Emory, and tries to start a business there with about $20, with the rule that he can't go home until he has doubled his money. After many door-to-door rejections he mows a lawn for $20 (tipped to $30), then sells $1 water outside a fair using price anchoring to reach $38. He also spots a brokerage-style opportunity: listing a rural man's old tractor and smoker online for a cut. Key takeaway: rural markets are hard, door-to-door is tough, and the most workable ideas are simple local services, selling-on-behalf for offline people, and arbitrage-style hustles. The title's '4 best rural side hustles' is not really delivered; it is an entertaining challenge video.

video.title: From Nothing to $20k/month with Email Newsletters: Full Tutorial

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jazz, who runs Winnipeg Digest, a local events/community newsletter (about 35,000 email subscribers plus about 73,000 social followers) started in April 2024. Jazz explains audience growth via Facebook ads, annual exclusive sponsorships priced at about $12,000 per year, survey-based audience data, and a VA plus Claude/ChatGPT content workflow. He is now vertically integrating by selling Christmas light installation to newsletter readers, with plans for permanent lights and a fractional-CMO-for-equity model. The key takeaway is that a local newsletter is a cheap audience asset to build, sponsor sales are the hard part, and the audience can be monetised further through owned businesses.

video.title: Watch This Overlooked AI Tool Build Me a Business in 23 Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates finding, validating and launching a business idea in one sitting using Replit Agent 3. He uses Google Trends and Google autocomplete to spot demand for free invoicing software for contractors, then vibe-codes an AI chat/email invoicing app with Stripe payment links and Resend email, and publishes it on a new domain (invoicefree.com). The app works after fixing email-domain verification, though emails land in spam. Key takeaway: search trends plus autocomplete are a cheap demand signal, and AI app builders can produce a working MVP in under an hour; Koerner says he does not plan to turn it into a business.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; builds the app live with Replit Agent 3

ideas.name: Invoice Freely: AI chat/email invoicing for contractors
ideas.one_liner: Free natural-language invoicing app where contractors text, email or chat a request and the customer gets an invoice with a Stripe payment link; revenue from a markup on card processing.
ideas.business_model: Free software monetised by a markup on Stripe card processing (about 0.5% on top of Stripe's 2.9%).
ideas.customer: Small businesses and contractors (tree trimmers, roofers, general contractors, home service businesses, gutter cleaners) who dislike filling in CRM/invoicing forms.
ideas.problem: Invoicing software is painful and rarely industry-specific; contractors on a job site do not want to log into a CRM and fill in name, phone, email and address.
ideas.offer: Free invoicing software where the user types or emails something like 'send an invoice for $800 to Mary Smith for tree trimming services'; the app extracts the details with OpenAI, asks for confirmation, and emails the customer an invoice with a Stripe checkout link. Includes a dashboard of invoices sent, paid and pending.

pricing.model: Free to users; platform earns a processing markup (e.g. 3.4% charged vs Stripe's ~2.9%); users can mark it up or pass it on
pricing.notes: The transcript garbles the figure ('3 12%'); read as roughly 3.4%, i.e. about half a percent on top of Stripe. Not a stated price to customers.

acquisition_channels.details: Host plans a lead capture / email capture / lead magnet on the site and exposure from this video; no real acquisition plan stated.

quote.text: I better get some sort of a lead capture, email capture, lead magnet on this because once this video goes live
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

summary: Side Hustle Nation host Nick Loper interviews Steve (App Masters, 17 years in app marketing, now acquiring and building vibe-coded apps). Steve's playbook: find keywords people search in the App Store (ASO), unbundle a feature from big apps, build a one-feature app named after the keyword, use a hard paywall with copied competitor pricing, and optionally run a lifetime-deal growth hack or Apple Search Ads. He claims apps earning from about $200/month to $35k MRR, and says roughly 40% of apps he launches make money. Key takeaway: distribution (ASO) matters more than features.
